# Organizing projects and data {#sec-organizing-projects}

**Core.** Work through it, with the exercises.

::: {.callout-note .goals icon=false}
## Learning goals

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Lay out a project folder that keeps raw data, reference, metadata,
   code, results, and logs apart, and name files so they sort well and
   avoid common path problems.
2. Verify downloaded files with checksums, and protect raw data from
   accidental changes and deletion.
3. Link shared data into a project with a symbolic link, and say what
   removing the link does and does not remove.
4. Record where every input and output came from (source, version,
   checksum, script, software version, log) in files kept in the project.
5. Say which of your storage locations are backed up, for how long, and
   who would restore them.
:::

## What this chapter does {#sec-organizing-projects-intro}

A month from now, someone (your PI, a reviewer, or you) will point at a
number and ask: which file is this, where did it come from, and how was
it made? If the answer lives only in your memory, it is already fading.
This chapter sets up a folder, and a few habits, that answer those
questions without memory.

You will turn `~/bioinf-computing`, the folder from @sec-book-setup, into the
book's project. By the end it holds:

- the two FASTQ files from @sec-orientation, moved in, checked, and
  protected from accidental changes;
- a reference genome kept in a shared folder and linked in, not copied;
- small tables that say which files belong to which sample;
- a numbered script that counts the reads and writes a log of every run;
- a README, a data record, and a notebook that say where everything came
  from.

Every later chapter starts from this folder. The commands are
copy-and-run, as in @sec-orientation; `mkdir`, `mv`, `ln`, `chmod` and
the rest are explained properly in Part II (@sec-shell-basics,
@sec-linux-system). Practice files, and anything broken on purpose, go
in a separate scratch folder, `~/bioinf-ch03`, never in the project.

## A folder for each project {#sec-organizing-projects-layout}

Do this on your laptop (in WSL2's Ubuntu terminal on Windows). Go to the
book folder and make the empty folders of the layout:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
mkdir -p data/raw data/meta src results logs # <1>
ls
```
1. `mkdir` makes folders; `-p` makes `data/` on the way to `data/raw`,
   and says nothing if a folder already exists.

```{.console}
data  logs  notes.txt  pixi.lock  pixi.toml  README.md  results  src
```

`pixi.toml` and `pixi.lock` are the book environment from
@sec-book-setup; `README.md` and `notes.txt` are your editor practice
from its exercises (delete `notes.txt` with `rm notes.txt` if you like).
The hidden `.pixi/` folder is there too; `ls -a` shows it.

@fig-project-layout shows where the chapter is going: the same folder
with every file it will hold by the end.

::: {#fig-project-layout}
{{< svg ../figures/project-layout.svg >}}

The book's project at the end of this chapter. Inputs (left) are never
changed by your work; code and software (middle) say how results are
made; outputs (right) are written by the script. The records along the
bottom explain all of it.
:::

The same project as text: this is what the `tree` command prints, run
inside `~/bioinf-computing` at the end of the chapter. `tree` comes with
the book environment, so start it with `pixi run`, as you did seqkit in
@sec-book-setup. Indentation shows
what is inside what, `->` marks a link and where it points, and the
last line counts what it found.

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
pixi run tree
```

```{.console}
.
├── data
│   ├── meta
│   │   ├── reads.tsv
│   │   ├── samples.tsv
│   │   └── samplesheet_upstream.csv
│   ├── raw
│   │   ├── checksums.md5
│   │   ├── SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
│   │   └── SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
│   ├── README.md
│   └── ref -> /home/you/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
├── logs
│   └── 01_count_reads_2026-11-17T122453_7WFs.log
├── NOTEBOOK.md
├── pixi.lock
├── pixi.toml
├── README.md
├── results
│   └── read_counts.tsv
└── src
    └── 01_count_reads.sh

7 directories, 15 files
```

`tree` sorts by name and, like `ls`, hides names that start with a dot,
so `.pixi/` is missing; `tree -a` shows it (and its thousands of files).
`tree -L 2` stops two levels down, which helps in big projects. Later
chapters use `tree` to show a tool's inputs and outputs; run it yourself
to check your folder against the book.

The rules behind it, one sentence each:

- **One project, one folder.** Everything an analysis needs, or points
  to, is inside it.
- **Inputs, code, and outputs apart.** Raw data and metadata in `data/`,
  scripts in `src/`, results in `results/`, logs in `logs/`. You never
  write into `data/raw/`, and nothing in `results/` is edited by hand.
- **Results can be rebuilt.** Everything in `results/` should come back
  if you rerun the code in `src/` on the inputs in `data/`, with the same
  software. Exercise 4 tests it.
- **Paths inside the project are relative to its top folder**
  (`data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz`, not `/home/you/bioinf-computing/data/…`),
  so scripts keep working if the folder moves (more on moving in
  @sec-organizing-projects-shared).

@tbl-project-folders lists the parts.

::: {.wide-table}
: The folders and files of the book's project. "Back it up?" is
discussed in @sec-organizing-projects-backups; git arrives in @sec-git. {#tbl-project-folders}

| Folder or file | What goes in it | Who writes it | Back it up? | In git later? |
|:---------------|:----------------|:--------------|:------------|:--------------|
| `data/raw/` | reads as received, and their checksums | you, once | yes | no (too big; archived elsewhere) |
| `data/meta/` | sample sheets and other metadata | you | yes | yes |
| `data/ref` | link to a shared reference | you, once | the shared copy: someone must | no |
| `src/` | numbered scripts | you | yes | yes |
| `results/` | tables and figures made by scripts | scripts | yes if costly to rebuild | usually not |
| `logs/` | one log per run | scripts | yes | small ones, often |
| `pixi.toml`, `pixi.lock` | the software (@sec-book-setup) | pixi | yes | yes |
| `.pixi/` | the installed environment | pixi | no: reinstall it | no |
| `README.md`, `NOTEBOOK.md`, `data/README.md` | what, why, where from | you | yes | yes |
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
Keep inputs, code, and outputs apart, so that every output can be
rebuilt from preserved inputs, code, settings, and software records. That
gives you the ingredients for reproducing an analysis; actually
rebuilding it is the test.
:::

This is one sensible layout, not the only one. @noble2009quick and
@wilson2017good describe close relatives; pipelines add a `work/` folder
of their own (@sec-workflow-managers), and later books adapt the layout
to their tools. What matters is that a stranger can find the raw data,
the code, and the results, and tell them apart.

**On a cluster** the same layout goes in project storage
(`/project/<your-project>/` on SCINet, `/work/<your-group>/` on Nova),
not in your small home folder or in scratch space that is purged
(@sec-book-setup-pixi). Large intermediate files may live in scratch
while a job runs, with only the final results kept in the project
(@sec-hpc-slurm). Making folders and moving files is light work, fine on
a login node; checksumming many large files is not.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** You delete `results/read_counts.tsv` by mistake (you
will make it later in this chapter). What do you need to get it back?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Nothing but the project itself: rerun the script on `data/raw/` with the
same environment. A large published analysis is different: rebuilding
it can take days of computing, or need a reference or a software version
that is no longer available, which is why important final results are
backed up too.
:::
:::

## Names that work {#sec-organizing-projects-names}

Start with a puzzle. In the scratch folder, make seven empty files with
names like the ones on many lab drives, then list them:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-ch03/names && cd ~/bioinf-ch03/names
touch run1.sh run2.sh run10.sh final.txt "Final FINAL (2).txt" "9-15-25 counts.csv" "10-2-26 counts.csv" # <1>
ls -1 # <2>
```
1. `touch` makes empty files. The quotes keep each name with spaces in
   one piece.
2. `-1` (the digit one) lists one name per line.

```{.console}
'10-2-26 counts.csv'
'9-15-25 counts.csv'
'Final FINAL (2).txt'
final.txt
run1.sh
run10.sh
run2.sh
```

(Captured on a Mac. On Linux with English language settings, `run10.sh`
comes before `run1.sh`; the order depends on the system's language
settings, but the two problems below appear everywhere.) `ls` sorts names character by
character, so `run10.sh` lands before `run2.sh`, and October 2026
(`10-2-26`) before September 2025 (`9-15-25`). `ls` puts quotes around
names with spaces to warn you, and spaces break commands that are not
quoted:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
wc -l 10-2-26 counts.csv
```

```{.console}
wc: 10-2-26: No such file or directory
wc: counts.csv: No such file or directory
0 total
```

The shell split the name at the space and looked for two files. Quoting
fixes it (`wc -l "10-2-26 counts.csv"`), and you will still learn to
quote paths (@sec-shell-basics), but names without spaces never need it.
@tbl-file-names gives the rules, each with a better name.

::: {.wide-table}
: Rules for file names, with the problem each one avoids. {#tbl-file-names}

| Rule | Problem name | Why it causes trouble | Better name |
|:-----|:-------------|:----------------------|:------------|
| Only letters, digits, `_`, `-`, `.` | `Final FINAL (2).txt` | spaces and brackets must be quoted in every command | `2026-11-17_read_counts.tsv` |
| One case, usually lowercase | `Data.csv` and `data.csv` | usually the same file on a Mac or in Windows folders, but two files on Linux, including your WSL home folder and the cluster | `data.csv` |
| Dates as `YYYY-MM-DD` ([ISO 8601](https://www.iso.org/iso-8601-date-and-time-format.html)) | `10-2-26 counts.csv` | sorts by month, not by time; day and month order is ambiguous | `2026-10-02_counts.csv` |
| Zero-padded numbers, scripts in run order | `run2.sh`, `run10.sh` | `run10` sorts before `run2` | `02_trim.sh`, `10_report.sh` |
| Say what is inside; keep the extension true | `results.txt` holding tabs | `.txt` hides that it is a table | `read_counts.tsv` |
| Versions say what changed | `final_v2.txt` | no one knows what v2 changed, or which is newest | `yeast_R64-1-1_test`, `report_2026-11-17.html`; later, git (@sec-git) |
:::

Number scripts in the order they run: `00_` for one-time setup such as
downloads, then `01_`, `02_`, …, so `ls src/` shows the analysis in
order. Two exceptions to renaming. First, IDs that come from a facility
or an archive (`SRR6357070`, `WT_REP1`) stay exactly as given, so they
still match the records; rename only your own files. Second, a name
whose meaning you do not know: is `11-3-25 counts.csv` 3 November or
11 March, 2025 or 2011? Renaming cannot recover what you do not know.
Ask whoever made it, then rename.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** In what order does `ls` list `run1.sh`, `run2.sh`,
and `run10.sh`, and how would you rename them?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`run1.sh`, `run10.sh`, `run2.sh` (on Linux, possibly `run10.sh` first;
`run2.sh` always comes after `run10.sh`). Pad the numbers and say what
each step does: `01_download.sh`, `02_trim.sh`, `10_report.sh`.
:::
:::

## Raw data: move it in, check it, protect it {#sec-organizing-projects-raw}

**Move it in.** The two FASTQ files from @sec-orientation are still in
the scratch folder `~/bioinf-ch01`. Move them into the project:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
mv ~/bioinf-ch01/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz ~/bioinf-ch01/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz data/raw/ # <1>
ls -l data/raw
```
1. `mv` moves files; the last name is where they go. Moving within one
   disk only changes where the file is listed, so it is instant.

```{.console}
total 4368
-rw-r--r-- 1 you you 2239317 Nov 17 11:22 SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
-rw-r--r-- 1 you you 2232117 Nov 17 11:22 SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
```

From now on the files live here: if you go back to a command in
Chapters 1–2, use `~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/` instead of `~/bioinf-ch01/`.
`~/bioinf-ch01` keeps `fastq_summary.txt`; you can delete it later.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Missing a file?
If `mv` says `cannot stat … No such file or directory` for a file (you
skipped the read-2 exercise, or deleted `~/bioinf-ch01`), the other file
still moved. Download each missing one straight into `data/raw/`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
curl -fL -o data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz {{< var testdata-url >}}/testdata/GSE110004/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
curl -fL -o data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz {{< var testdata-url >}}/testdata/GSE110004/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
```

Run only the line for the file you are missing. If a file is already in
`data/raw/` from an earlier visit to this chapter, leave it: the check
below tells you whether it is intact.
:::

**Check it.** A sequencing facility, or an archive such as ENA, gives
you a checksum for every file: a short value computed from every byte of
it. Here are the MD5 checksums of the two files, as the book recorded
them. Make a file `data/raw/checksums.md5` (`code
data/raw/checksums.md5` opens it in VS Code; nano works too), paste the
two lines, and save:

```{.default filename="data/raw/checksums.md5"}
d19f3c7a8b4016fa641458257b99a1a1  SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
d126cc66ed169f69af2c07da0dd73e02  SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
```

Each line is a checksum, two spaces, and a file name. Now check the
files against it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd data/raw
md5sum -c checksums.md5 # <1>
cd ~/bioinf-computing
```
1. `md5sum` computes MD5 checksums; `-c` (check) reads a list of them,
   recomputes each file's, and compares.

```{.console}
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: OK
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: OK
```

The names in `checksums.md5` have no folder, so the check runs inside
the folder that holds the files. Facilities ship their lists the same
way. Run it from the wrong folder and every file "fails":

```{.console}
md5sum: SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: FAILED open or read
md5sum: SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: FAILED open or read
md5sum: WARNING: 2 listed files could not be read
```

**Now name the idea** (@fig-checksum). A checksum is a fingerprint of a
file: the same bytes always give the same value, and changing a single
byte gives a completely different one. A matching checksum means your
copy is byte-for-byte the file the checksum was made from.

::: {#fig-checksum}
{{< svg ../figures/checksum.svg >}}

Checksums of the real read-1 file. An exact copy gives the same MD5
value; changing one byte out of 2,239,317 (`6a` to `6b`, halfway
through) gives a completely different value.
:::

Run `md5sum -c` after every download or transfer, before any analysis
(@sec-working-remotely reuses it after copying to a cluster). Two kinds
of failure mean different things:

- **`FAILED`**: the bytes differ, usually an incomplete or damaged copy.
  Download or copy the file again and recheck. Never "fix" the list by
  computing a new checksum from the damaged copy.
- **`FAILED open or read`** with `No such file or directory`: the file
  is missing, misnamed, or you are in the wrong folder. Check that
  before assuming damage.

`sha256sum` works the same way (`sha256sum -c`) with a longer, stronger
value (both are documented in the [GNU coreutils
manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/html_node/md5sum-invocation.html)); the book's own `data/README.md` records both. MD5 is still what
most facilities and ENA supply, and it is fine for catching damaged
copies.

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "If the checksums match, my data are correct"
**Reality.** A match proves your copy is identical to the file the
checksum was made from. It says nothing about whether that file was the
right sample, or good data: if a facility mislabels a file before
computing its checksum, `md5sum -c` happily prints `OK`.
:::

**Protect it, first on a toy.** Raw data is never edited, so make it
read-only. Try it first on a practice folder with one small file:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-ch03/practice/locked && cd ~/bioinf-ch03/practice
echo "first line" > locked/notes.txt
chmod a-w locked/notes.txt locked # <1>
echo "second line" >> locked/notes.txt # <2>
rm -f locked/notes.txt # <3>
mv locked/notes.txt notes_moved.txt
touch locked/new.txt
```
1. `chmod` changes a file's permissions; `a-w` removes (`-`) write
   permission (`w`) for all users (`a`). Here it locks both the file and
   the folder that holds it.
2. Try to add a line, then (next lines) to delete the file, move it out,
   and add a new file.
3. `-f` deletes without asking. Without it, `rm` may stop to ask about
   a read-only file; a job running unattended cannot answer.

```{.console}
bash: locked/notes.txt: Permission denied
rm: cannot remove 'locked/notes.txt': Permission denied
mv: cannot move 'locked/notes.txt' to 'notes_moved.txt': Permission denied
touch: cannot touch 'locked/new.txt': Permission denied
```

All four were refused. Why lock the folder too? Deleting, moving, and
adding files change the folder's list of names, so the folder's
permission controls them, not the file's. A read-only file in a
writable folder can still be deleted:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p open && echo "first line" > open/notes.txt
chmod a-w open/notes.txt
rm -f open/notes.txt
ls open
```

`rm -f` printed nothing and `ls` shows an empty folder: the read-only
file is gone. (Without `-f`, `rm` asks before deleting a read-only file
when its input is a terminal, even from a script you started there. With
`-f`, or in a job running unattended, nothing asks.)

**Now protect the real raw data**, files and folder:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
chmod a-w data/raw/* data/raw
ls -ld data/raw # <1>
ls -l data/raw
```
1. `-d` lists the folder itself instead of its contents.

```{.console}
dr-xr-xr-x 2 you you 4096 Nov 17 11:22 data/raw
total 4372
-r--r--r-- 1 you you     112 Nov 17 11:22 checksums.md5
-r--r--r-- 1 you you 2239317 Nov 17 11:22 SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
-r--r--r-- 1 you you 2232117 Nov 17 11:22 SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
```

The `w` letters are gone. This guards against accidents (a script that
writes to the wrong path, a slip of `rm`), not against you: as the
owner you can always give write permission back. To add a file later,
unlock the folder and the checksum list (the existing reads can stay
locked), add the file and its line from the source's checksum list,
check, and lock everything again:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
chmod u+w data/raw data/raw/checksums.md5
# add the new file and its line in checksums.md5, then:
cd data/raw && md5sum -c checksums.md5 && cd ~/bioinf-computing
chmod a-w data/raw/* data/raw
```

 @sec-linux-system explains
permissions properly. Keep raw reads compressed, and never unzip them in
place: every tool in this book reads `.gz` directly.

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
Raw data is read-only: check it once with checksums, protect it, and
never edit it. Every change happens in a script that writes somewhere
else.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** `md5sum -c` prints `FAILED` for a file you just
copied from the cluster. What happened, and what do you do? What if it
says `FAILED open or read`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`FAILED`: your copy's bytes differ from the original, usually an
incomplete transfer. Copy it again and recheck; do not analyse it.
`FAILED open or read`: the file is missing or misnamed, or you ran the
check from the wrong folder.
:::
:::

## Shared data: link, don't copy {#sec-organizing-projects-shared}

On a cluster, a lab keeps one copy of each reference genome and big
shared dataset in a shared folder, something like
`/project/<lab>/references/`, and every project points to it. No one
copies a 3 GB genome into each project, and no one's quota pays twice.
You will make a **stand-in** for such a folder in your home folder and
link it into the project.

**Make the shared folder.** Download the test genome (yeast chromosome I
only, 71 kB) and its annotation into it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
cd ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
curl -fLO {{< var testdata-url >}}/reference/genome.fa.gz
curl -fLO {{< var testdata-url >}}/reference/genes.gtf.gz
```

Give it a checksum list, as the person who set up the folder would:

```{.default filename="~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test/checksums.md5"}
4222a07bf01b12782245e0ff774459fe  genome.fa.gz
504334f6741ee771c665ae845429087f  genes.gtf.gz
```

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
md5sum -c checksums.md5
```

```{.console}
genome.fa.gz: OK
genes.gtf.gz: OK
```

And a README, so anyone who finds the folder knows what it is:

```{.markdown filename="~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test/README.md"}
# Yeast test reference (stand-in for a lab's shared references)

- genome.fa.gz: S. cerevisiae R64-1-1, chromosome I only (one sequence, >I)
- genes.gtf.gz: matching gene annotation (test subset)
- Source: nf-core/test-datasets, rnaseq branch, folder reference/,
  commit 9dd6d014f560e182047992834a8d267214fbccd1
- Downloaded: 2026-11-17 (write your date)
- Checksums: checksums.md5 (MD5)
- License: MIT (nf-core/test-datasets)
```

Then protect the folder, as a lab would protect its shared references:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
chmod a-w ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test/* ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
```

**Link it into the project:**

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
ln -s ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test data/ref # <1>
ls -l data/ref
ls data/ref/
```
1. `ln -s target name` makes a symbolic link called `name` that points
   to `target`.

```{.console}
lrwxrwxrwx 1 you you 53 Nov 17 11:22 data/ref -> /home/you/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
checksums.md5  genes.gtf.gz  genome.fa.gz  README.md
```

`ls -l` shows the link itself: an `l` at the start, and an arrow to the
path it holds (on a Mac the path starts with `/Users/`). `ls data/ref/`,
with the slash, looks through the link and lists the shared folder's
files.

**Now name the idea** (@fig-symlink). A **symbolic link** (symlink) is
another route to the same data, not a copy: a tiny entry that holds only
a path. Programs that open `data/ref/genome.fa.gz` read the file in the
shared folder.

::: {#fig-symlink}
{{< svg ../figures/symlink.svg >}}

What a symbolic link is, and what each action does to it. Use *Next* to
step through.
:::

See both halves of that on a toy link in the practice folder (never on
the real reference). Writing through a link writes to the original, and
removing the link leaves the original alone:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-ch03/practice
mkdir -p target && echo "original line" > target/note.txt
ln -s target toylink
echo "added through the link" >> toylink/note.txt
cat target/note.txt
unlink toylink # <1>
ls
cat target/note.txt
```
1. `unlink` removes one link (or file) and nothing else.

```{.console}
original line
added through the link
locked  open  target
original line
added through the link
```

The line written through `toylink` landed in `target/note.txt`; after
`unlink`, the link is gone and the target still holds both lines. (Try
the same write on `data/ref/README.md` and you get `Permission denied`:
the protection you added to the shared folder stops it, as step 3 of
@fig-symlink shows.) A link whose target is moved or renamed is
**broken**: `ls -l` still shows the arrow (in red in many terminals),
and opening a file through it says `No such file or directory`.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: `rm -r data/ref/` deletes the shared data
Remove a link with `unlink data/ref` or `rm data/ref`: no slash at the
end, no `-r`. With a trailing slash, which {{< kbd Tab >}} completion
adds for you, `rm -r` follows the link. On a Mac with GNU coreutils 9.11
(and with macOS's own `rm`), this deleted the entire shared folder
without a word, and left the link behind, now broken:

```{.console}
$ rm -r proj/ref/
$ echo $?
0
$ ls -l proj
total 0
lrwxr-xr-x 1 you staff 20 Nov 17 11:34 ref -> /home/you/shared/ref
$ ls -A shared/ref
ls: cannot access 'shared/ref': No such file or directory
```

(Captured in a test folder, with `$` before each command: `echo $?`
prints `0`, the code for success, and the shared folder `shared/ref` is
gone.) On Linux (Ubuntu 24.04, GNU coreutils 9.4) the result differs but
is no better: `rm` deleted every file inside the shared folder, then
stopped with `rm: cannot remove 'proj/ref/': Not a directory`, leaving
the folder empty.

Do not run this. The shared folder you made survives it only because
you protected it: `rm` then stops with `Permission denied`. A lab's real
shared folder may not be protected from you.
:::

**Moving the project.** Relative paths in scripts let the project move,
but a link is only a pointer: copy the project to another machine (say,
laptop to cluster) and `data/ref` points at a path that does not exist
there. Moving a project means three steps: copy the project's files;
reinstall the environment from `pixi.toml` and `pixi.lock`
(@sec-book-setup); and recreate `data/ref` to point at that machine's
copy of the same reference, which `data/README.md` identifies by source,
release, and checksums (@sec-organizing-projects-provenance). Transfer
commands come in @sec-working-remotely. And a link is not a backup of
its target: someone (you, the lab, or the site) must look after the
shared copy (@sec-organizing-projects-backups). Which genome release to
use, and why chromosome names differ between sources, is
@sec-reference-data.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** You run `unlink data/ref`. Is the reference genome
gone? What must you do to use the project on a second machine?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
No, only the link is gone; the shared folder is untouched. On the second
machine, recreate the link to that machine's copy of the same
reference, identified by its source, release, and checksums in
`data/README.md`, and reinstall the environment from the lockfile.
:::
:::

## Backups: where do your files really live? {#sec-organizing-projects-backups}

Start with a question for each place you keep files: if you deleted a
file there by mistake today, could you get it back? @tbl-storage-backup
answers it for a laptop and the two clusters this book uses as examples.
Copy its rows for your own storage into your notebook (you will start it
in @sec-organizing-projects-records) and fill them in from your site's
documentation.

::: {.wide-table}
: Is it backed up? Site facts from SCINet's [storage
guide](https://scinet.usda.gov/guides/data/storage) and ISU's [HPC file
storage guide](https://research.it.iastate.edu/file-storage), checked
2026-11-17, and Nova's login banner (@sec-book-setup-ssh); your site's own pages are the authority, and policies change
(@sec-cluster-sites). "Not stated": the site's guide does not say. {#tbl-storage-backup}

| Storage | Example path | Backed up? | Purged? | Who restores a deleted file |
|:--------|:-------------|:-----------|:--------|:----------------------------|
| Laptop disk | `~/bioinf-computing` | only if you set up a backup | no | you, from your backup |
| Sync folder (OneDrive, Dropbox, Google Drive) | `~/OneDrive/…` | no: a copy that follows your changes | no | you, from version history, for as long as it is kept |
| SCINet home | `/home/<user>` (30 GB) | no: "Cluster storage is not backed up" | not stated | no one |
| SCINet project | `/project/<project>` | no (same rule) | not stated | no one |
| SCINet 90-day scratch | `/90daydata/<project>` | no | files older than 90 days, permanently | no one |
| SCINet Juno | (long-term storage) | the place to back up data that "cannot be easily reproduced" | not stated | not stated |
| Nova home | `/home/<netid>` (10 GB) | not stated | not stated | not stated |
| Nova group work | `/work/<group>` | daily snapshots, 7 kept | not stated | the file-system admins: ask ISU support |
| Nova scratch | `/ptmp/<you>` | no | files not used for 60 days | no one |
| Nova Large Scale Storage | `/lss/research/<group>` | yes, per Nova's login banner ("a backed-up system like /lss") | not stated | ask ISU support |
| A compute node's local disk | `$TMPDIR` | no | at the end of each job | no one |
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: scratch is purged and not backed up
Files in scratch space (`/90daydata`, `/ptmp`) are deleted
automatically; on SCINet the deletion "is permanent and the files cannot
be recovered". Use scratch for
files a job can make again, copy results you need into project storage,
and find out which other areas are backed up, and for how long, before
you trust them.
:::

**Then name the rule: 3-2-1.** Keep three copies of anything you cannot
recreate, on two kinds of storage, with one somewhere else (off site).
For raw sequence data, the facility's copy or the public archive (SRA or
ENA, once you have submitted) can be one of the three, but only if you
know it is kept and for how long. An archive of the original reads does
not preserve a subset or a fix you made yourself.

A few points the table makes:

- **Cluster storage is often not a backup at all.** SCINet says so for
  all of its cluster storage, and scratch is purged everywhere. Even
  storage with snapshots (Nova's `/work`) should not be your only copy:
  Nova's login banner says so.
- **A sync folder copies your mistakes too.** Delete or overwrite a file
  and the change syncs everywhere. It is one copy in two places, unless
  version history is kept and you know for how long.
- **Git keeps the history of code** (@sec-git), but only a copy stored
  somewhere else, such as a remote repository (@sec-github), protects it
  if your machine is lost.

What to back up: raw data, metadata, code, the notebook, logs, and the
records that explain results; important final results too. A result you
can rebuild in seconds, such as this chapter's read counts, needs no
backup of its own. A large or published analysis may need days of
computing, a reference that is no longer online, or an old software
version to rebuild, so keep it. Intermediate files that a pipeline can
make again can follow a lighter rule. And test a restore once: a backup
you have never restored from is a hope, not a backup.

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "My Dropbox (or OneDrive) folder is my backup"
**Reality.** Sync copies deletions and overwrites to every device. It
protects you only through version history, for as long as the service
keeps it, which you need to check.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** Your raw FASTQ files are in cluster scratch and in a
OneDrive folder on your laptop. Is that a backup you can rely on? What
would you check?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Not as it stands: scratch is purged and not backed up, and OneDrive
copies deletions. Check how long OneDrive keeps old versions, whether
the facility or SRA keeps the original reads (and for how long), and put
a copy in storage that is backed up.
:::
:::

## Sample sheets and metadata {#sec-organizing-projects-metadata}

Reads mean nothing without knowing which sample each file came from.
That knowledge is **metadata**, and it lives in tables. Start with the
sample sheet nf-core uses to test its RNA-seq pipeline, kept with the
book's reads in [nf-core/test-datasets](https://github.com/nf-core/test-datasets/tree/rnaseq). Download it into `data/meta/` and keep it exactly as
it came, under a name that says so:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
curl -fL -o data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv {{< var testdata-url >}}/samplesheet/v3.10/samplesheet_test.csv
md5sum data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv
code data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv
```

```{.console}
fb28ab0a8cda268b2befd974804b2925  data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv
```

The checksum matches the one in the book's `data/README.md`, so you have
the same file. Its contents, with the long download addresses shortened
to `…/` (the real file has the full URL of each FASTQ file):

```{.default filename="data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv (shortened)"}
sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,strandedness
WT_REP1,…/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz,…/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz,auto
WT_REP1,…/SRR6357071_1.fastq.gz,…/SRR6357071_2.fastq.gz,auto
WT_REP2,…/SRR6357072_1.fastq.gz,…/SRR6357072_2.fastq.gz,reverse
RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP1,…/SRR6357073_1.fastq.gz,,reverse
RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2,…/SRR6357074_1.fastq.gz,,reverse
RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2,…/SRR6357075_1.fastq.gz,,reverse
RAP1_IAA_30M_REP1,…/SRR6357076_1.fastq.gz,…/SRR6357076_2.fastq.gz,reverse
```

Look before reading on. There are 7 rows but only 5 sample labels:
`WT_REP1` and `RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2` each have two rows. Three rows have
an empty `fastq_2`, so those runs are given as single-end. And a
`strandedness` column says how each library was made. In this sheet
each row is one sequencing run, with its mate files; rows that share a
label are merged into one sample by the pipeline (@sec-nf-core).

**Now check the labels against the source.** The runs are public, so
the archive has a record for each. The European Nucleotide Archive's
records ([ENA](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/browser/view/SRR6357070), for
the first run) (checked 2026-11-17)
tell a different story: the seven runs are **seven different biological
samples** (GSM2879618 to GSM2879624), and all seven were sequenced
paired-end (@fig-sample-sheet). The two `WT_REP1` runs are wild-type
replicates 1 and 2; the sheet's `WT_REP2` is replicate 3.

::: {#fig-sample-sheet}
{{< svg ../figures/sample-sheet.svg >}}

The test sample sheet beside the archive record. The sheet groups 7 runs
under 5 labels and gives three as single-end; ENA lists 7 biological
samples, all paired-end. Only SRR6357070's two files are in this
project.
:::

Nothing is wrong with the sheet: it is a pipeline **test fixture**.
Its labels group runs so the test exercises merging and single-end
input; they were never meant to describe the experiment. The lesson is
general. A sample label is a claim: check it against the source record,
and never infer the biology from names alone. (How to design an
experiment with replicates is the Transcriptomics book's subject.)

**Now the project's own metadata**, for the files actually in
`data/raw/`. Two small tables, one per question. `reads.tsv` says which
files belong to which run and sample; `samples.tsv` says what each
sample is, from its archive record. These commands write them, one line
at a time (`printf` prints its text, `\t` is a tab, `\n` ends the line;
`>` starts the file and `>>` adds to it, as in @sec-orientation):

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
printf 'sample\trun\tfastq_1\tfastq_2\n' > data/meta/reads.tsv
printf 'WT_REP1\tSRR6357070\tdata/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz\tdata/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz\n' >> data/meta/reads.tsv
printf 'sample\trun\tgeo_sample\tcondition\treplicate\n' > data/meta/samples.tsv
printf 'WT_REP1\tSRR6357070\tGSM2879618\twild_type\t1\n' >> data/meta/samples.tsv
cat data/meta/reads.tsv data/meta/samples.tsv
```

```{.console}
sample  run     fastq_1 fastq_2
WT_REP1 SRR6357070      data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz  data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
sample  run     geo_sample      condition       replicate
WT_REP1 SRR6357070      GSM2879618      wild_type       1
```

(The columns are separated by tabs, which the terminal shows as jumps
to the next multiple of 8 characters, so they do not line up. Open the
files in VS Code to see them as columns.) A real project has one
row per run in `reads.tsv` and one per sample in `samples.tsv`; the
`sample` column is how the two tables join (@sec-tabular-data).

**Now name the idea.** Metadata is data, not a note on the side: kept
beside the reads, checked, and changed only on purpose. The rules:

- One row per run (or per sample), one column per property.
- Plain CSV or TSV files, not spreadsheets with merged cells, colour
  coding, or notes in the margins (spreadsheet pitfalls:
  @sec-tabular-data).
- Sample IDs are spelled the same in every table: `WT_REP1` in one and
  `WT_rep1` or `WT_REP1 ` (with a trailing space) in another are
  different IDs.
- File-path columns point at the right files. Sample IDs and file names
  need not match (`WT_REP1` and `SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz`): the table is
  what connects them.
- Values come from the source record, with the record's ID
  (`GSM2879618`) kept so anyone can check them.

nf-core's own sample-sheet format, and how it merges runs, are covered
in @sec-nf-core.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** The upstream sheet has two rows labelled `WT_REP1`.
Are they two runs of one biological sample? How would you find out?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Not here: ENA lists them as different biological samples, wild-type
replicates 1 and 2. The test sheet groups them to test merging. Check
the archive record, not the label.
:::
:::

## Provenance: where did this number come from? {#sec-organizing-projects-provenance}

In @sec-orientation you typed a read count into `fastq_summary.txt` by
hand. Nothing in that file says which file was counted, with what, or
when. Now make a result that records how it was made.

**Add the script.** Open a new file in VS Code (`code
src/01_count_reads.sh`), paste the script below, and save. You run it in
this chapter; @sec-shell-scripts explains every line.

```{.bash filename="src/01_count_reads.sh"}
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# 01_count_reads.sh: check the raw FASTQ files, then count their reads.
# Run from the project folder:  pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh
set -euo pipefail

mkdir -p results logs
log="$(mktemp "logs/01_count_reads_$(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H%M%S)_XXXX.log")"

{
  echo "started:  $(date "+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z")"
  echo "host:     $(hostname)"
  echo "script:   $(md5sum src/01_count_reads.sh)"
  echo "seqkit:   $(seqkit version)"
  echo "checking inputs against data/raw/checksums.md5:"
  (cd data/raw && md5sum -c checksums.md5)
  echo "command:  seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz"
  seqkit stats --quiet -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz > results/read_counts.tsv.tmp
  mv results/read_counts.tsv.tmp results/read_counts.tsv
  echo "output:   $(md5sum results/read_counts.tsv)"
  echo "finished: $(date "+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z")"
} 2>&1 | tee "$log"
```

**Run it** from the project folder, through pixi, so it finds seqkit:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh
```

```{.console}
started:  2026-11-17 12:24:53 -0600
host:     your-laptop
script:   76fa8eb6a7b90f212042cfbe6d95cfcc  src/01_count_reads.sh
seqkit:   seqkit v2.14.0
checking inputs against data/raw/checksums.md5:
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: OK
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: OK
command:  seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz
output:   e1d81de77934f7ab7b44bf72b7520b32  results/read_counts.tsv
finished: 2026-11-17 12:24:53 -0600
```

Your date, time, host, and log name will differ. Then look at what it made:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cat results/read_counts.tsv
ls logs
```

```{.console}
file    format  type    num_seqs        sum_len min_len avg_len max_len
data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz  FASTQ   DNA     50000   5050000 101     101.0   101
data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz  FASTQ   DNA     50000   5050000 101     101.0   101
01_count_reads_2026-11-17T122453_7WFs.log
```

(Tab-separated again: `-T` asks seqkit for a plain table that other
programs can read, without the commas and aligned columns of
@sec-book-setup. `num_seqs` is 50,000 in each file.) What the script did, in plain words:

1. Checked the inputs against `checksums.md5`, and would have stopped
   there if any failed.
2. Recorded the date, the machine, the script's own checksum, the
   seqkit version, and the command.
3. Counted the reads into a temporary file, and only then moved it into
   `results/`. A run that fails half-way cannot replace a good result
   with an empty one.
4. Recorded the output's checksum.
5. Saved everything it printed, including any messages from seqkit, in
   a new log in `logs/`, named by date and time plus four random
   characters (`_7WFs`; `mktemp` picks a name no other file has), so
   every run keeps its own log, even two runs in the same second.

The log is the run's record. A log with no `finished:` line means the
run failed, and its last lines say where (@sec-getting-help starts from
exactly that). When one input was corrupted on purpose, the run stopped
at `FAILED`, kept the old result, and left the failure in its log.

**Record where the inputs came from.** The log says what the script
read; `data/README.md` says where those files came from. Make it from
this template (the book keeps the same record for its own data):

```{.markdown filename="data/README.md"}
# Data in this project

## Raw reads: data/raw/

- Files: SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz, SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz (paired-end, read 1 and read 2)
- What: S. cerevisiae RNA-seq, run SRR6357070 (GEO sample GSM2879618,
  wild type, biological replicate 1), sub-sampled to 50,000 read pairs
  by nf-core for testing
- Source: {{< var testdata-url >}}/testdata/GSE110004/
- Accessions: GEO GSE110004; SRA run SRR6357070
- Downloaded: 2026-11-13 (Chapter 1; write your own date)
- Checksums: data/raw/checksums.md5 (MD5). SHA-256:
  3f50541fa9cf2bedc87e7b682ada0fccfdfcd6d27b9bb81f17be230ff140ebe7  SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
  8590e1e01e568fba256aa7dced40519604cbb111ee44ab106a3dcb869660aaf4  SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
- License: MIT (nf-core/test-datasets); original reads public in SRA
- Cite: Wu et al. (2018), Molecular Cell 72(6), 942-954.e7,
  doi:10.1016/j.molcel.2018.10.018

## Reference: data/ref (a link)

- Points to: ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test (see its README.md)
- What: S. cerevisiae R64-1-1, chromosome I only, with gene annotation (test subset)
- Source: {{< var testdata-url >}}/reference/
- Checksums (MD5):
  4222a07bf01b12782245e0ff774459fe  genome.fa.gz
  504334f6741ee771c665ae845429087f  genes.gtf.gz
- On another machine: link data/ref to a copy with these checksums

## Metadata: data/meta/

- samplesheet_upstream.csv: nf-core's test sheet, unchanged.
  Source: {{< var testdata-url >}}/samplesheet/v3.10/samplesheet_test.csv
  MD5 fb28ab0a8cda268b2befd974804b2925
- reads.tsv: which local files belong to which run and sample (written by hand)
- samples.tsv: what each sample is, from its ENA record (checked 2026-11-17)
```

`{{< var testdata-url >}}` is the full download address, pinned to one
commit of nf-core/test-datasets, so the files at that address can never
change.

**Now name the idea** (@fig-provenance-chain). **Provenance** is the
record of where something came from. For `read_counts.tsv`, every link
in the chain is now in the project.

::: {#fig-provenance-chain}
{{< svg ../figures/provenance-chain.svg >}}

The provenance of `results/read_counts.tsv`. The code, the software, the
inputs it read, and the log of the run point to the result; the inputs
point back to their sources. The reference and the upstream sample
sheet are project records, but this result did not read them.
:::

@tbl-provenance-record lists what to record and where it lives.

: What to record for each result, and where it lives in the book's
project. {#tbl-provenance-record}

| What to record | In this project | Where it lives |
|:---------------|:----------------|:---------------|
| Source of each input | download address, commit, accession, date | `data/README.md` |
| Exact input files | MD5 of each file | `data/raw/checksums.md5`, checked in the log |
| Code | `src/01_count_reads.sh` and its MD5 | `src/`, the log |
| Command and options | `seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz` | the log |
| Software versions | seqkit v2.14.0; every package | the log; `pixi.lock` |
| When, where, what happened | start and end times, host, check results | the log |
| The output | `read_counts.tsv` and its MD5 | `results/`, the log |
| Why, and what went wrong | decisions and dead ends | `NOTEBOOK.md` (next section) |

Most of this costs nothing if you record it when the file is made, and
is impossible to rebuild later. Later chapters add to the chain: git
commits for the script (@sec-git), parameters and random seeds
(@sec-environments), and pipeline versions and reports (@sec-nf-core).

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
Record provenance when the file is made: source, version, checksum,
script, command, software, log. It costs a minute now and cannot be
rebuilt later.
:::

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "I'll remember where this file came from"
**Reality.** Weeks later no one does, including you. A file whose source,
version, and making are not written down cannot be trusted, and often
cannot be used in a paper.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** A reviewer asks which version of seqkit made
`read_counts.tsv`. Where in the project is the answer?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
In the run's log in `logs/` (the `seqkit:` line), and in `pixi.lock`.
:::
:::

## Writing it down: README, notebook, FAIR {#sec-organizing-projects-records}

**The README.** Open `README.md` from @sec-book-setup and replace its
two lines with an outline like this one. It answers the first questions
a stranger (or you, in a year) will ask:

```{.markdown filename="README.md"}
# Computing for Bioinformatics: book project

Worked project for the book *Computing for Bioinformatics*. Counts the
reads in one yeast RNA-seq run; later chapters add to it.

## Layout

- data/raw/   reads as received, read-only; checksums in checksums.md5
- data/meta/  sample sheets and metadata
- data/ref    link to the shared reference (see data/README.md)
- src/        scripts, numbered in run order
- results/    made by the scripts; can be rebuilt
- logs/       one log per run

## Data

Where every input came from: data/README.md.

## How to rerun

    pixi install --locked
    pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh

## Software

pixi.toml and pixi.lock (installed with pixi 0.84.2).
```

**The notebook.** A script shows what was done; it does not show why,
what you tried first, or what went wrong. That goes in a notebook. Make
`NOTEBOOK.md` in the project and give it a first dated entry:

```{.markdown filename="NOTEBOOK.md"}
# Notebook

## 2026-11-17

- Organized the project (Chapter 3): moved the reads from ~/bioinf-ch01
  into data/raw/, checked them with md5sum -c (both OK), made them read-only.
- Linked the test reference from ~/bioinf-shared/ instead of copying it.
- The nf-core test sheet groups 7 runs under 5 labels, but ENA lists
  7 biological samples, all paired-end: the labels are a test grouping.
  Used the ENA record for samples.tsv.
- Ran src/01_count_reads.sh: 50,000 reads in each file.
- Next: ...
```

Newest entries go at the bottom (or the top: pick one and keep to it).
Write a few lines each day you work: what you did, why, what went
wrong, and what is next. A plain Markdown file in the project is the
book's default; if your lab already uses an electronic lab notebook,
use that. The habit matters, not the tool.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Markdown in one box
`README.md` and `NOTEBOOK.md` are **Markdown**: plain text with a few
marks. `#` starts a heading (`##` a smaller one), `-` starts a list
item, and backticks mark code (`` `md5sum -c` ``). VS Code shows a
preview with {{< kbd Cmd-Shift-V >}} ({{< kbd Ctrl-Shift-V >}} on Windows
and Linux). Quarto (@sec-r-essentials) uses the same marks; see its
[Markdown basics](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html).
:::

**FAIR, briefly.** Funders and journals increasingly ask for data that
is **FAIR**: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable
[@wilkinson2016fair]. @tbl-fair shows which habits from this chapter
support each principle.

::: {.callout-note}
## Background: the FAIR principles

: The FAIR principles [@wilkinson2016fair], and habits from this
chapter that support them. {#tbl-fair}

| Principle | What it means | Habits from this chapter that support it |
|:----------|:--------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Findable | Data have persistent identifiers and rich metadata, so they can be found | citing accessions (`SRR6357070`, `GSM2879618`, `GSE110004`) in `data/README.md` |
| Accessible | Anyone can learn how to get the data, by a standard method; access may need a login | download addresses pinned to a commit; where each input came from |
| Interoperable | Data use standard formats and shared vocabularies | FASTQ, FASTA, and GTF files; plain CSV/TSV metadata with clear columns |
| Reusable | Data come with a license, provenance, and enough description to be used again | the license and citation for each input; checksums, logs, and the README |
:::

A README and a tidy CSV do not by themselves make a project FAIR; that
takes depositing data, with good metadata, in an archive that gives it
identifiers (@sec-reference-data, @sec-github). They make it much
easier. And Accessible does not have to mean open to everyone: data
behind a login are fine, as long as how to get access is clear. More on
FAIR at [GO FAIR](https://www.go-fair.org/fair-principles/).

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** Which FAIR principle does citing `SRR6357070` and
`GSE110004` in your README support?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Findable, through persistent identifiers (and Reusable, since others can
trace and credit the data).
:::
:::

## Summary {#sec-organizing-projects-summary}

- One project, one folder, with inputs (`data/`), code (`src/`), and
  outputs (`results/`, `logs/`) apart, so results can be rebuilt. Names
  without spaces, ISO dates, zero-padded numbers, scripts numbered in
  run order.
- Raw data is checked with `md5sum -c` (in the folder that holds the
  files) after every download or transfer, then protected with
  `chmod a-w` on the files **and** the folder. `FAILED` means damaged;
  `FAILED open or read` means missing or the wrong folder.
- Shared data is linked, not copied: `ln -s target data/ref`. Remove a
  link with `unlink data/ref`, never `rm -r data/ref/`. A link does not
  travel with the project; `data/README.md` says what to link on another
  machine.
- Each result has a record of its provenance: the inputs' sources and
  checksums (`data/README.md`, `checksums.md5`), the script, the
  software (`pixi.lock`), and a log of every run. `README.md` and
  `NOTEBOOK.md` say what the project is and why you did what you did.
- Know which of your storage is backed up, for how long, and who
  restores it. Scratch is purged; a sync folder copies mistakes;
  3-2-1 for anything you cannot recreate.

The project now looks like this:

```{.default}
~/bioinf-computing/
├── README.md
├── NOTEBOOK.md
├── pixi.toml  pixi.lock  .pixi/
├── data/
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── raw/        SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz  SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz  checksums.md5
│   ├── meta/       reads.tsv  samples.tsv  samplesheet_upstream.csv
│   └── ref -> ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
├── src/            01_count_reads.sh
├── results/        read_counts.tsv
└── logs/           01_count_reads_2026-11-17T122453_7WFs.log
```

## Exercises {#sec-organizing-projects-exercises}

Practice files go in `~/bioinf-ch03/`, not in the project.

::: {.check}
**Exercise 1. Rename a messy folder.** Make a folder of badly named
files:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-ch03/messy && cd ~/bioinf-ch03/messy
touch "SRR6357070 R1.fastq.gz" "Analysis.R" "plot 1.png" "plot 2.png" "plot 10.png" "counts final.txt" "counts final_v2.txt" "11-3-25 notes.txt"
```

`counts final.txt` and `counts final_v2.txt` are really tab-separated
tables, and `_v2` added one sample. Write down a new name for each file,
then rename them with `mv`, quoting the old names, for example:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mv "plot 1.png" plot_01.png
```

What would you ask before renaming `11-3-25 notes.txt`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
One good set:

| Old name | New name | Why |
|:---------|:---------|:----|
| `SRR6357070 R1.fastq.gz` | `SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz` | no space; keep the archive's ID and its `_1` convention |
| `Analysis.R` | `01_analysis.R` | lowercase; numbered in run order (better: say what it analyses) |
| `plot 1.png`, `plot 2.png`, `plot 10.png` | `plot_01.png`, `plot_02.png`, `plot_10.png` | zero-padded, so they sort 1, 2, 10 |
| `counts final.txt` | `counts_7samples.tsv` | true extension; says what it holds |
| `counts final_v2.txt` | `counts_8samples.tsv` | says what changed, instead of `v2` |
| `11-3-25 notes.txt` | ask first | |

Now `ls -1` lists the plots in order. For the date, ask whoever wrote
it: is it 3 November or 11 March, and which year? Then rename to
`2025-11-03_notes.txt` or `2025-03-11_notes.txt` (or the right year).
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 2. Catch a broken transfer.** Make a truncated copy of read 1
in the practice folder, as an interrupted transfer would, copy the
checksum list beside it, and check:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-ch03/practice
head -c 1000000 ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz > SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
cp ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/checksums.md5 .
md5sum -c checksums.md5
gzip -t SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
```

(`head -c 1000000` keeps the first million bytes. Read 2 is missing on
purpose.) Which kind of failure does each file give? Both checks catch
this copy; which one would catch a file that is complete, but the wrong
sample?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

```{.console}
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: FAILED
md5sum: SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: FAILED open or read
md5sum: WARNING: 1 listed file could not be read
md5sum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match
gzip: SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: unexpected end of file
gzip: SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: uncompress failed
```

Read 1 is `FAILED` (bytes differ); read 2 is `FAILED open or read`
(missing). `gzip -t` catches truncation too. Only the checksum, compared
against the facility's list, catches a wrong file that is still valid
gzip. Neither tells you whether the facility's own file was right
(the misconception in @sec-organizing-projects-raw).
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 3. Labels against records.** Here are the ENA records for all
seven runs in the upstream sheet (captured 2026-11-17 from ENA's
[file report](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/) for each run):

| Run | GEO sample | Sample title | Layout |
|:----|:-----------|:-------------|:-------|
| SRR6357070 | GSM2879618 | Wild-type total RNA-Seq biological replicate 1 | PAIRED |
| SRR6357071 | GSM2879619 | Wild-type total RNA-Seq biological replicate 2 | PAIRED |
| SRR6357072 | GSM2879620 | Wild-type total RNA-Seq biological replicate 3 | PAIRED |
| SRR6357073 | GSM2879621 | Rap1-AID degron no induction total RNA-Seq biological replicate 1 | PAIRED |
| SRR6357074 | GSM2879622 | Rap1-AID degron no induction total RNA-Seq biological replicate 2 | PAIRED |
| SRR6357075 | GSM2879623 | Rap1-AID degron no induction total RNA-Seq biological replicate 3 | PAIRED |
| SRR6357076 | GSM2879624 | Rap1-AID degron induction 30 minutes total RNA-Seq biological replicate 1 | PAIRED |

Copy the upstream sheet into the practice folder (`cp
~/bioinf-computing/data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv ~/bioinf-ch03/`), open
the copy in VS Code, and add `geo_sample` and `condition` columns from
this table. How many biological samples are there? How many runs are
really paired-end? Why might a test fixture group them differently? And
what goes wrong if a sample ID in one table has a trailing space?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Seven biological samples, all paired-end. The fixture's labels exist to
test the pipeline: two labels with two runs each test merging, and three
runs given as read 1 only test single-end input. A trailing space makes
a different ID (`WT_REP1 ` is not `WT_REP1`), so the two tables fail to
match when joined; @sec-tabular-data shows how to detect it.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 4. Rebuild and compare.** Save a copy of the result outside
`results/`, delete `results/`, rerun the script, and compare:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cd ~/bioinf-computing
cp results/read_counts.tsv ~/bioinf-ch03/read_counts_before.tsv
rm -r results
pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh
cmp ~/bioinf-ch03/read_counts_before.tsv results/read_counts.tsv # <1>
ls logs
```
1. `cmp` compares two files byte by byte and prints nothing if they are
   identical.

Then add a `NOTEBOOK.md` entry for today.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
`cmp` prints nothing: the rebuilt result is identical. `logs/` now has
two logs, one per run, with different names, which is why outputs
and logs are kept apart. The result could be deleted safely because the
inputs, code, and software records were all kept.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 5. Your own storage.** (Cluster readers.) Make the same
layout in your project storage, link a reference your site or lab
already provides (@sec-cluster-sites) or the test reference, and fill in
the rows of @tbl-storage-backup for your site from its documentation,
including who restores a deleted file. No cluster yet? Fill in the rows
for your laptop and any sync folder you use.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Answers depend on the site. A complete row names the path, whether it is
backed up or snapshotted and for how long, whether it is purged and
after how long, and whom to ask (with the link to the page you used).
If the documentation does not say, write "not stated" and ask your
site's support rather than assume.
:::
:::

## Further reading {#sec-organizing-projects-reading}

- @wilson2017good, "Good enough practices in scientific computing" ---
  the closest match to this chapter: data management, project
  organization, and keeping track of changes, as a short checklist.
- @noble2009quick, "A quick guide to organizing computational biology
  projects" --- the classic project layout and lab-notebook advice;
  compare its folders with ours.
- @wilkinson2016fair --- the paper that defined the FAIR principles; read
  the box of principles, not the whole paper.
- @shotts2025linux, *The Linux Command Line*, the chapters on links and
  on permissions --- for readers who want `ln` and `chmod` explained
  before @sec-shell-basics and @sec-linux-system.
